title: CrashLoopBackOff — Image Pull Failure
remediation_steps: Check the image name and tag in the pod spec — verify it exists in the registry
Run 'kubectl describe pod <pod>' and look at the Events section for pull errors
Verify image pull secrets are configured if using a private registry
Check if the image tag was recently changed (kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>)
Rollback to the previous working image: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>
If the image is correct, check network connectivity to the container registry
escalation_criteria: Escalate if the image tag was intentionally changed and the registry is confirmed accessible — may indicate a build/publish pipeline issue.

title: CrashLoopBackOff — Application Error
remediation_steps: Check pod logs: kubectl logs <pod> --previous (for crashed containers)
Look for application startup errors, missing config, or dependency issues
Check if environment variables or ConfigMaps are correctly mounted
Verify volume mounts and secrets exist and are accessible
Check if there was a recent config change: kubectl rollout history
If config-related, fix the ConfigMap/Secret and redeploy
If code-related, rollback to previous version: kubectl rollout undo
escalation_criteria: Escalate if logs show an unknown error or if the same version was previously working — may indicate an environmental change.

title: OOMKilled — Container Memory Limit Exceeded
remediation_steps: Check the container's memory limits: kubectl describe pod <pod>
Query Prometheus for memory usage trends: container_memory_working_set_bytes
Determine if memory usage is growing over time (memory leak) or spiking
If memory leak: investigate application code, check for known memory leak issues
If legitimate load increase: increase memory limits in the deployment spec
As a quick fix, increase memory limits: kubectl patch deployment/<name> -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"<container>","resources":{"limits":{"memory":"256Mi"}}}]}}}}'
Monitor after increase to verify stability
escalation_criteria: Escalate if memory usage grows linearly over time (memory leak pattern) — requires application-level fix.

title: OOMKilled — JVM Heap Misconfiguration
remediation_steps: Check if JVM heap size (-Xmx) is set appropriately relative to container memory limit
JVM heap should be ~75% of container memory limit (leave room for non-heap memory)
Check GC logs for excessive garbage collection
Update JAVA_OPTS or JVM_OPTS to set -Xmx appropriately
Increase container memory limit if the JVM genuinely needs more heap
Consider enabling -XX:+UseContainerSupport for JVM container awareness
escalation_criteria: Escalate if the JVM is configured correctly but still OOMing — may indicate a memory leak in the application.

title: Failed Rollout — Readiness Probe Failure
remediation_steps: Check deployment rollout status: kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>
Describe the new pods to see readiness probe failures in events
Verify the readiness probe path and port match the application's health endpoint
Check if the new image actually serves on the expected port
Check for startup time issues — increase initialDelaySeconds if the app takes longer to start
Rollback to the previous version: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>
Fix the readiness probe configuration and redeploy
escalation_criteria: Escalate if the probe config is correct but pods still fail readiness — may indicate an application startup issue.

title: Failed Rollout — Missing ConfigMap or Secret
remediation_steps: Check events for specific ConfigMap/Secret name that is missing
Verify the ConfigMap/Secret exists in the correct namespace: kubectl get configmap -n <ns>
If it was deleted accidentally, recreate it from source or backup
If it was renamed, update the deployment spec to reference the new name
Rollback if the ConfigMap/Secret change was part of the failed deployment
escalation_criteria: Escalate if the ConfigMap/Secret was deleted by an automated process or pipeline.

title: Failed Rollout — Resource Quota Exceeded
remediation_steps: Check resource quota status: kubectl describe resourcequota -n <namespace>
Compare requested resources with quota limits
Option 1: Reduce resource requests in the deployment spec
Option 2: Request a quota increase for the namespace
Option 3: Scale down other deployments in the namespace to free resources
Rollback the deployment while waiting for quota adjustment
escalation_criteria: Escalate if quota increase requires platform team approval.

title: Pods Pending — Insufficient Node Resources
remediation_steps: Check which resources are insufficient: kubectl describe pod <pod> (look at Events)
Check node resource usage: kubectl top nodes
Check if any nodes are cordoned or have taints: kubectl get nodes -o wide
Option 1: Reduce resource requests in the pod spec
Option 2: Scale up the cluster (add more nodes)
Option 3: Evict or scale down lower-priority workloads
Check for node affinity or anti-affinity rules that may be too restrictive
escalation_criteria: Escalate if cluster autoscaler is not responding or if all nodes are at capacity.

title: Pods Pending — PersistentVolumeClaim Issues
symptoms: waiting for a volume to be created
remediation_steps: Check PVC status: kubectl get pvc -n <namespace>
If PVC is Pending, check if a matching PV exists or if dynamic provisioning is configured
Check the StorageClass: kubectl get storageclass
Verify the CSI driver is running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi
Check cloud provider quota for disk volumes
If using a specific PV, check if it is Available and has matching capacity/access mode
escalation_criteria: Escalate if the storage backend is experiencing issues or if cloud provider quota is exhausted.

title: Service Connectivity Issues — DNS Resolution Failure
remediation_steps: Check CoreDNS pods are running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
Test DNS resolution from a pod: kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local
Check CoreDNS logs for errors: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
Verify the Service exists and has endpoints: kubectl get endpoints <service> -n <namespace>
Check if the Service selector matches the pod labels
Restart CoreDNS if it is unresponsive: kubectl rollout restart deployment/coredns -n kube-system
escalation_criteria: Escalate if CoreDNS is crashlooping or if cluster-wide DNS is broken.

title: High Pod Restart Count
remediation_steps: Check restart count: kubectl get pods -n <namespace>
Check previous container logs: kubectl logs <pod> --previous
Check pod events: kubectl describe pod <pod>
Determine if restarts are caused by: OOMKill, liveness probe failure, application crash, or exit code
Check liveness probe configuration — it may be too aggressive
If OOMKill: see runbook RB-003
If application crash: see runbook RB-002
escalation_criteria: Escalate if restart count exceeds 50 in the past hour or if restarts are accelerating.

title: High Latency / Slow Responses
remediation_steps: Check current CPU and memory utilization: kubectl top pods -n <namespace>
Query Prometheus for request latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))
Check if pods are CPU throttled: container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total
Check HPA status: kubectl get hpa -n <namespace> — may need to scale out
Check for upstream dependency issues (databases, external APIs)
If CPU throttled: increase CPU limits or add more replicas
If memory pressure: check for GC pauses (JVM) or memory swap
escalation_criteria: Escalate if latency affects SLO/SLA thresholds or if the root cause is an upstream dependency.

title: Node Not Ready
remediation_steps: Check node status: kubectl get nodes -o wide
Describe the NotReady node: kubectl describe node <node>
Check kubelet status on the node (if accessible): systemctl status kubelet
Check for disk pressure, memory pressure, or PID pressure conditions
Check cloud provider console for instance health
If the node is truly unrecoverable, drain it: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
Replace the node via cluster autoscaler or manually
escalation_criteria: Escalate if multiple nodes are NotReady simultaneously — may indicate a control plane or networking issue.

title: CrashLoopBackOff — Readiness/Liveness Probe Misconfiguration
remediation_steps: Check probe configuration: kubectl describe pod <pod>
Verify the probe endpoint is correct (path, port, scheme)
Check if the application needs more time to start — increase initialDelaySeconds
Check if the probe timeoutSeconds is too short for the application
Test the probe endpoint manually: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl -s localhost:<port>/<path>
Consider adding a startupProbe for slow-starting applications
Temporarily remove the probe to verify the application is running correctly
escalation_criteria: Escalate if the probe config matches the application's actual health endpoint — may indicate an application health issue.

title: Deployment Scaled to Zero Replicas
remediation_steps: Check current replica count: kubectl get deployment <name> -n <namespace>
Check HPA if present: kubectl get hpa -n <namespace>
Check if the scale-down was intentional (maintenance, cost saving)
Scale back up: kubectl scale deployment/<name> --replicas=<desired> -n <namespace>
Check HPA minReplicas if HPA is managing the deployment
Review recent events for manual or automated scale-down actions
escalation_criteria: Escalate if the scale-down was not intentional and affects a production service.
